extracted.intended_audience: trademark attorneys, IP professionals, and brand owners (Japan-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating likelihood of confusion between trademarks under Japanese law (JPO guidelines and IP High Court practice), focusing on similarity, fame/distinctiveness, relatedness of goods, consumer overlap, and business diversification/licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of similarity between the filed trademark and the other person's mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how similar the contested mark and the cited mark are in overall impression, including pronunciation and appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IPHC pointed out high degree of similarity in terms of pronunciation and the appearance of the trademarks; similarity in pronunciation and look can be decisive in finding likelihood of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of the other person's mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how well-known or recognized the cited mark is among consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-known/famous trademark increases the likelihood of confusion; the Court noted the cited trademark was a well-known famous trademark and highly creative, which weighed in favor of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the other person's mark consists of a coined word or has distinctive features in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate distinctiveness of the cited mark (e.g., coined words, unique composition) as a factor in confusion analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks that are coined or have distinctive composition receive stronger protection—distinctiveness makes consumer association likelier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the other person's mark is their company's mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the cited mark is used as a company mark, which can affect the assessment of source confusion and breadth of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company marks may be entitled to broader protection; the Guidelines list this as a specific criterion to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of business diversification of the other person
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the owner of the cited mark could or does expand into other goods/services (licensing, business diversification) that would make overlap with the contested mark more likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court observed that some designated goods of the contested mark had relevance to goods/business where the cited-mark owner grants licenses; evidence or realistic possibility of diversification/licensing increases chance of confusion or mistaken affiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativeness among goods or services (relatedness of goods/services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge how closely related the goods or services designated by each mark are, including functional or use-based connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatedness among goods/services raises the risk of confusion. The Guidelines explicitly list 'relativeness among goods or services or between goods and services' as a key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonality of consumers and actual situation of deal
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the consumers/clients for the respective goods/services overlap (e.g., general consumers vs. specialized professional purchasers) and real-world transactional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guidelines cite 'commonality of consumers of goods, etc. and other conditions such as actual situation of deal'—while Taguchi argued its consumers were specialized civil-engineering firms, the Court considered market realities and licensing that could blur consumer distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of misunderstanding about economic or organizational relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether consumers may think the goods/services originate from the cited mark's business or from a business economically/organizationally related (affiliate, licensee, group) to the cited mark owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO Guidelines define 'likely to cause confusion' to include not only mistaken origin but also mistaken belief that the product relates to a business which belongs to someone who has some economical or organizational relationship with the other person. The IPHC found risk that consumers might believe designated goods were offered by parties with close business partnerships or a group commercializing identical marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standard: trademark likely to cause confusion under JPO Guidelines (Article 4(1) & Article 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the JPO Trademark Examination Guidelines' definition and enumerated criteria (degree of similarity; recognition; distinctiveness; company mark; business diversification; relatedness of goods/services; commonality of consumers/transactional circumstances) when assessing likelihood of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guidelines frame the inquiry as both (a) possible misunderstanding that the goods/services belong to the other person's business and (b) possible misunderstanding that the goods relate to a business economically/organizationally connected with the other person. Use the listed factors collectively to reach a conclusion; the Court relied on multiple factors (similarity, fame, related goods/licensing) to invalidate GUZZILLA.
